full_judgment:
Mohammad Gholam Rabbani J: This Rule brings a point of some importance. The point is that while deciding an application under section 5 of the Limitation Act for condonation of delay caused by the Government what yardstick is to be followed. 

 2. Section 5 runs as follows: "Any appeal or application for a revision or a review of judgment or for leave to appeal or any other application to which this may be made applicable by or under any enactment for the time being in force may be admitted after the period of limitation prescribed thereof, when the appellant or applicant satisfies the court that he had sufficient cause for not preferring the appeal or making the application within such period." 

 6. We are in agreement with this decision of the Single Bench. There is no doubt about the legal position that the law of limitation operates equally for or against the private party and also on the Government. But it is a fact which must be accepted that a private litigant is normally presumed to be aware of all the factors and aspects of his case and he has only to make up his own mind as to pursue further his litigation whereas in the case of Government a longer time is required for enquiry and consideration vis-a-vis public interest by not only one agency, but several ones before taking final decision and thereafter acting thereon. Thus period of time which may be sufficient for private litigant may not be so for the Government. The Court is to consider in the case of the latter whether a Government department in question has acted bonafide or has been grossly negligent in prosecuting its case and if the Court comes to the conclusion that there has been no gross negligence the Court should condone the delay disregarding the length of the delay. 

 9. Mr. SS Halder, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, submits that the learned District Judge ought to have considered this decision together with the subsequent decision of a Division Bench reported in 1991 BLD 194 wherein delay of 260 days in filing an appeal by the Government was not condoned holding that the delay was due to gross negligence and laches. The fact of the case in this decision is distinguishable from that of the instant case. In that case delay was not condoned as the application for condonation of the delay had not explained at all the reasons for such delay whereas in the instant case reasons for delay were specifically stated. The learned District Judge in the exercise of his discretion under section 5 of the Limitation Act accepted the reasons for delay and accordingly, condoned the delay.
